source_read: Saved PubMed Central page text (PMC4418947, author manuscript), read in full: abstract, unheaded Introduction, all headed sections, Figure 1–4 legends (the figures are images), highlights and acknowledgements; bibliography checked for the cited studies (142 entries).

anchors.locator: Structural Brain Imaging of Methamphetamine Users, 6th paragraph; Figure 2 title and legend
anchors.extracted: In vervet monkeys given a methamphetamine regimen that the reviewers describe as resembling a common human pattern of use (escalating, per the Figure 2 title), putamen grey matter increased (striatal increase p<0.05 corrected against saline, Figure 2 legend), and the increase was associated with reductions in D2-type receptor and DAT availability and with poorer cognitive flexibility (Groman et al., 2013, as summarized). No magnitudes and no data on persistence are given.
anchors.note: The original extraction is not wrong but leaves out what makes this a qualifier for a claim about use as people use it: the regimen is presented as resembling human use, and the D2/DAT reductions as associated with the grey-matter increase. Elsewhere the review cites recovery of D2-type receptor availability with protracted abstinence in monkeys (Groman et al., 2012; Molecular Imaging › Monoamine systems, 4th paragraph).

for_senior_author: Risk of bias: re-appraised today by AI reader 3 with the editors' narrative-review checklist (overall high); reader 2's 'agree' was given to the superseded AMSTAR 2 rating. Domain judgments not re-judged here.

Interpretation gap: reader 2 agrees (substantial) and would add to 'claimed' the authors' neurotoxicity framing (now key finding 15) and the Introduction's statement that imaging studies have demonstrated corticostriatal dysfunction in people who use methamphetamine (2nd paragraph; confirmed). Interpretation-gap text unchanged.
